w: What's tested Carious vs noncarious cervical lesions: the same place on the tooth, a different cause The three causes of NCCLs, alone or together: abrasion (toothbrushing), abfraction (occlusion) and erosion (acid) Abrasion: the toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush; relative dentin abrasivity (RDA); soft brushes, less pressure and the dominant-side clue The evidence that not every NCCL comes from toothbrushing Abfraction: why a load on an inclined plane makes a lesion at the cervical area (compression, tension and the fulcrum), its clues and the night guard Erosion vs caries, where vomiting erodes and why, pH vs buffering capacity, and which drinks are worst Matching the treatment to the cause, and when an NCCL needs a restoration 1 Three causes, alone or together: abrasion, abfraction and erosion; carious vs noncarious A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Carious vs noncarious cervical lesions: the same place, a different cause. Carious ones are soft and brown, and resin-modified glass ionomer is a great option for them. Three causes, alone or together: abrasion (toothbrushing), abfraction (occlusion) and erosion (acid). Match the fix to the cause: a lower-RDA toothpaste, then a pressure-sensor brush; a less acidic drink and bicarbonate; a night guard. A lot of plaque can sit at the cervical area of a tooth, so caries-mediated lesions form there. They look like caries: soft and brown. They are difficult to restore, sitting under the gums in a patient at risk for caries, and a great option for them is resin-modified glass ionomer. Noncarious cervical lesions are in the same location but have a completely different etiology: they are caused by factors that are not caries. His first slide puts the two side by side: the carious lesion is soft-looking brown tooth structure, while a noncarious one can be brown too but looks hard. Abrasion Toothbrushing, above all the toothpaste A lower-RDA toothpaste; if it's already low, less pressure, with an electric toothbrush that has a pressure sensor Abfraction Occlusion: loads on the occlusal surface flex the tooth A night guard (occlusal splint) to grind on instead of the teeth Erosion Acid sitting on the teeth A less acidic drink; bicarbonate to raise the mouth's pH; perhaps a water rinse 2 Abrasion: the toothpaste matters more than the brush; RDA (higher is more abrasive) A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this RDA (relative dentin abrasivity): higher is more abrasive, so recommend a low-RDA toothpaste. Relative dentin abrasivity (RDA) rates how abrasive a toothpaste is: the higher the number, the more abrasive, and the lower the number, the less. Recommend toothpastes with lower numbers. His slide adds that a toothpaste's RDA must be below 250 to get the ADA seal. On his chart, a Colgate whitening toothpaste is about 124, and Crest Pro-Health is always very high. You used to have to look a toothpaste up on a list; now you can ask an AI chatbot, which (live in the recording) gave the same 124 as the chart. Toothbrushing: switch to a lower-RDA toothpaste. If it's already low, the patient may be pressing too hard: an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor. 3 Not every NCCL is from brushing: leprosy, archaeological, animals, the palate, subgingival A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this People with leprosy who couldn't brush, archaeological populations, animals, and lesions on the palate and below the gum line. Studies of populations with leprosy, people unable to brush their own teeth, found NCCLs. NCCLs form where a toothbrush doesn't easily go: on the palate, where people don't usually brush, and even subgingivally, where the bristles can't reach. 4 Abfraction: an inclined-plane load, weaker in tension, the lesion just above the fulcrum A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Abfraction: a load on an inclined plane flexes the tooth about the fulcrum at the bone; the lesion forms on the tensile side, just above it (the stop sign). How can a load on the occlusal surface make a lesion on the side of the tooth, at the cervical area? Studies using finite element analysis (FEA), the stress images on his slide, show that loads on the inclined planes of the occlusal surface cause stress at the cervical part of the tooth. In materials science, things are almost always stronger in compression than in tension (being pulled apart). A load the tooth isn't supposed to have, on an inclined plane, pushes the crown to one side. The fulcrum is where the tooth is anchored in the bone. One side of the tooth is compressed; on the other side, tensile forces pull apart the bonds within the tooth structure, and where those tensile stresses are, abfraction lesions can form, just above the fulcrum. 5 pH vs buffering capacity: high is bad; orange juice and wine; citric acid chelates calcium A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Ranked by buffering capacity, orange juice and wine get much worse, and citric acid chelates calcium: ask a patient with erosion about citrus drinks. A dental student in their lab (later a resident, now an endodontist) measured both for a whole range of beverages. Ranked by buffering capacity, the drinks stayed in about the same order as by pH, with two exceptions: orange juice and wine became "way, way bad." On his slide their pH is about 3.6 and 4.0, not the lowest on the chart (the most acidic drink is 2.5), yet they took the most bicarbonate to neutralize. People drink orange juice all the time, so for a patient with a lot of erosion, ask about citrus drinks. Citric acid is a chelator: it wraps around calcium, so citrus drinks and citrus fruit can be extremely erosive to enamel. 6 Match the treatment to the cause (his last slide) A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank What to do: an occlusal splint, a night guard (he apologizes in advance to Dr. Givan if that isn't the right term). This one isn't treating TMD: it is a piece of plastic between the patient's teeth, so they grind a sacrificial piece of plastic instead of their teeth. Any of these lesions can also be restored for esthetic reasons if needed. Acid: switch to a less acidic drink; rinse with water after meals (he doesn't know of evidence for it); bicarbonate, such as Basic Bites. Abfraction: a night guard. 7 When to restore: cleansable, doesn't hurt, doesn't look bad, not deep A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Restore an NCCL when it can't be cleaned, hurts, looks bad or is deep, near the pulp (what he learned in school, "not official"). What he learned in dental school (not official, he says): you don't necessarily need to restore an NCCL if it is cleansable, doesn't hurt, doesn't look bad and isn't so deep that it is getting close to the pulp. A lesion that can't be cleaned, hurts, looks bad or is deep is the one to restore. 8 The clues: dominant side for brushing; tori and wear facets for abfraction Core of the lecture · 5 questions in the bank Know this Abrasion worse on the dominant side points to the toothbrush (lesions on the left only: ask if they're left-handed). For abfraction: a night guard, sacrificial plastic, not a TMD treatment. Its clues: exostoses and tori, opposing wear facets, generalized wear. The dominant-side clue. People push harder on the side of their dominant hand, while on the other side they have to pull. So abrasion that looks worse on the patient's dominant side than on the other side points to the toothbrush. A patient with abrasion lesions on the left side but not the right? Ask, "Are you left-handed?" Those are the patients to coach on brushing more gently, perhaps with an electric toothbrush with a sensor. How would you know a lesion is abfraction and not abrasion? "It's hard to know," but look for clues that the patient loads their teeth heavily: exostoses and tori sometimes accompany NCCLs, along with opposing wear facets or other generalized wear that shows the patient is wearing their teeth. 9 Erosion vs caries, and where vomiting erodes Core of the lecture · 6 questions in the bank Know this Vomiting erodes the lingual of the maxillary teeth, mostly the anteriors. In a sense all destruction of teeth comes down to acid: a cavity is lactic acid dissolving enamel. But caries is bacteria-mediated demineralization, so it occurs only where plaque stagnates: the cervical areas of the teeth, around orthodontic brackets, the occlusal grooves, and proximally just below the contact point. Erosion happens wherever acidic fluids sit, and it isn't the same as caries. Vomiting (bulimia, or anyone who throws up a lot) erodes the lingual of the maxillary teeth, mostly the anterior teeth: the facial surfaces are protected by the lip, and the lingual of the mandibular teeth by the tongue. And when acidic fluids sit at the cervical area of the teeth, they make noncarious cervical lesions. 10 Water dilutes, bicarbonate neutralizes (pH is a log scale) A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Why water may help less than he'd like: pH is on a logarithmic scale. In the lab, doubling an acid with water doesn't meaningfully change its pH; you'd need "a swimming pool of water." To neutralize an acid before pouring it down the sink, you add a base, such as bicarbonate. Water is fine, just probably not as effective as he wishes. Checking the mouth's pH with pH strips isn't easy either: his own saliva always reads about neutral. Also flagged in class The toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush: ask a patient with abrasion about their toothpaste. A soft brush protects the gums too. For pressure: brush more gently, or use an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor. Buffering capacity: how much bicarbonate (saliva) it takes to neutralize a drink. High is bad, low is good. pH is read with a probe; buffering capacity, by adding bicarbonate until the pH is neutral. Sparkling water: more bubbles, more acid. Milk makes coffee less acidic, and tea is better than coffee. Water only dilutes; a base (bicarbonate: a baking soda rinse, Basic Bites) neutralizes. You can skip Low-pH mouth rinses: probably not a big deal. Acidic drinks only at mealtimes, a straw, a water rinse afterward: sensible, but unproven.
